text: Augustine's famous remark — “What then is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I want to explain it to one that asks, I do not know” — is used in the book to capture which feature of the problem of time?
choices: The gap between our fluent, pre-theoretical familiarity with time and our inability to give a theoretical account of what it is
The claim that time does not exist at all, since neither the past nor the future is real
The relativistic discovery that clocks run at different rates in different reference frames
The thesis that time is nothing over and above the relations among events
explanation: The book reads Augustine's remark as naming the gap between knowing-how (using temporal concepts fluently) and knowing-that (stating what time is) — a lived familiarity that resists conceptual capture. Denying time's existence is Aristotle's aporia, not Augustine's point here; frame-dependent clocks belong to special relativity; and 'nothing over and above relations' is Leibniz's relationalism, each discussed elsewhere in the unit.
